new_statements.quote: c) Akzent und Ton. Der dynamische Ton ruht offenbar stets auf der vorletzten Silbe, auch wo dieselbe nicht (erste) Stammsilbe ist, vgl. z. B. ibeza »Brust«, mhogö »Büffel« zu ndiögolö »Hahn«. In mwenge »acht« liegt wohl Schreib- oder Hörfehler für musikalischen Ton, Hochton vor, vgl. das Folgende. Von musikalischen Tönen sind von Meinhof ausschließlich Hochtöne der Auslautsilben beobachtet worden. new_statements.translation: c) Accent and tone. The dynamic tone [= stress accent] evidently always rests on the penultimate syllable, even where that syllable is not the (first) stem syllable, cf. e.g. ibeza 'breast', mhogö 'buffalo' beside ndiögolö 'cock'. In mwenge 'eight' there is probably a writing or hearing error for musical tone, high tone; cf. the following. Of musical tones Meinhof observed exclusively high tones on final syllables. [p. 105:] Long final syllables occur only in monosyllabic stems; the prefixes are lengthened by the accent (namely before monosyllabic stems).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (stress) accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, regardless of morphological structure (it can fall on a prefix before a monosyllabic stem, which is then lengthened); separately, the language has musical (pitch) tones, with high tones noted on final syllables. Modern work (Boyd 2020; Meeussen 1974; McCawley 1973) treats Bangubangu as a two-tone H/L language with rightward tone shift and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: mwenge 'eight' apparently accented on the final syllable, which Struck explains away as a transcription/hearing error for a final high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from a roughly 70-item wordlist that Meinhof elicited on 2 Jan 1903 at Wilhelmstal (Usambara, German East Africa) from one displaced speaker named Wanga, compared with older travellers' vocabularies (Stanley, Livingstone); Struck himself never heard the language. Confidence in the statement is therefore low despite being first-hand in print.
new_statements.identity_note: Struck 1913 calls the language 'Mbangubangu' and explicitly identifies it with the Bangubangu (Bangobango) of the Kasongo-Kabambare region, i.e. bang1350; his data come from a single speaker recorded far from the language area, dialect unknown. Boyd 2020 covers the bangubangu dialects lusangi (reference dialect, Ludindi sector), wamaza, salamabila, kabambare and bahemba/mikebwe, plus nonda and shuula treated as separate languages; she suggests the 'bahemba' variety is really a dialect of Hemba [hem] rather than Bangubangu. Meeussen 1953/1954 recorded Bangubangu at Lusangi and Mutingwa (Ludindi sector).

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (no 'accent', 'tonique', 'pénultième' anywhere in the chapter). §2.2 pp. 461-462: 'Le bangubangu a un système tonal à deux tons : Haut (H) et Bas (B)'; verbs in two tone classes, nominal stems with four melodies B, BH, HB, H; the tone of nouns and verbs shifts one syllable (or mora) to the right, default B on prefixes; open syllables only, five short and five long vowels, long vowels partly conditioned by NC or glide (p. 450-451).
